title: Hangover Pills at CVS and Walgreens: What to Buy (and Skip)
excerpt: A pharmacy-aisle guide to hangover pills at CVS and Walgreens: which pain relievers, stomach remedies, and electrolytes help, what to skip, and how to avoid doubling up.
metaDescription: Hangover pills at CVS and Walgreens: which pain relievers, stomach aids, and electrolytes help, what to skip, store brands, and how to avoid doubling up.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
Nothing at CVS or Walgreens fixes a hangover, and most of what's sold for one is a familiar pain reliever, antacid or electrolyte drink in different packaging. The store-brand versions of those basics contain the same active ingredients for less. For the morning after, buy an electrolyte drink, one pain reliever chosen for your symptoms, something for your stomach if it's upset, and food. If you want a supplement aimed at drinking itself, such as DHM, you'll usually have to order it online.

Below: what's in each aisle, what's worth the money, what to skip, the ingredient overlaps that catch people out, and the symptoms that mean you need a doctor rather than a basket.

> **This is not medical advice.** Most of the products in this guide are over-the-counter drugs with real interactions with alcohol and with other medicines. Read every Drug Facts label, and **talk to your doctor or the pharmacist behind the counter** before taking anything if you take prescription medicine, are pregnant, have a stomach, liver, kidney, heart, or bleeding condition, or drink heavily most days. **Get medical help right away (call 911 in the US) if** someone can't stay awake, is confused, is vomiting repeatedly and can't keep water down, has slow or irregular breathing, has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, or bluish skin. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, not a hangover, and no store product will fix them. If you think someone took too much of a medicine, call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** (US).

## What Counts as a "Hangover Pill" at CVS and Walgreens

What people buy for a hangover at a pharmacy falls into four groups, and it helps to know which one you need before you walk in.

1. Pain relievers for the headache and body aches: acetaminophen (Tylenol), ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), naproxen (Aleve) and aspirin, plus combinations such as Alka-Seltzer, Excedrin and Blowfish.
2. Stomach products for nausea, heartburn and diarrhea: Pepto-Bismol and its store brands, Tums and other antacids, famotidine (Pepcid), and motion-sickness tablets.
3. Rehydration products: oral electrolyte solutions like Pedialyte and the CVS Health and Walgreens equivalents, and powders like Liquid I.V.
4. "Hangover" or "recovery" supplements: vitamin blends, milk thistle and the occasional branded hangover formula. These are dietary supplements, not drugs.

The first two groups are FDA-regulated drugs with tested doses. The third is well supported for the dehydration part of a hangover. The evidence for the fourth runs from thin to none, and it's where most of the marketing lives.

Stock varies a lot by store. A big-city flagship might have a "hangover" end cap while a small branch has only the basics, and both chains list far more online than they keep on the shelf. If you want something specific, check the app for in-store stock before you go.

## The Best Hangover Pills at CVS, Aisle by Aisle

The aisles below are in order of how likely each is to help.

### Electrolytes first (the beverage and baby aisles)

Alcohol makes you pee more because it suppresses vasopressin, a hormone that tells your kidneys to hold on to water. Add sweating, a short night and maybe vomiting, and you can wake up properly low on fluid. Water helps, but an oral rehydration drink with sodium and a little sugar is absorbed more efficiently, which is why oral rehydration solutions are used medically.

At CVS you'll typically find:

- **Pedialyte** in the baby aisle (and often near the cooler), including the higher-electrolyte AdvancedCare Plus versions and powder packs.
- **CVS Health electrolyte solution**, the store brand, which usually costs noticeably less than Pedialyte and has a similar formula. Compare the sodium and potassium on the labels and you'll see how close they are.
- **Liquid I.V.** and other electrolyte powder sticks, usually in the vitamin or beverage aisle.
- **Sports drinks** like Gatorade, which have less sodium and more sugar than an oral rehydration solution but are fine for mild dehydration.

If you only buy one thing, make it this. For a deeper comparison, see our guides to [Pedialyte vs Gatorade for a hangover](/never-hungover/pedialyte-vs-gatorade-hangover) and [whether Liquid I.V. helps a hangover](/never-hungover/liquid-iv-for-hangover).

### Pain relievers (the pain relief aisle)

This is where most of the "hangover pill" shopping happens, and where the most important safety decisions are. CVS stocks every major brand plus CVS Health versions of each, which contain the same active ingredient at the same dose for less.

- **Ibuprofen or naproxen** (Advil, Motrin, Aleve, CVS Health ibuprofen and naproxen). These are usually the most helpful for a hangover headache, because inflammation plays a part in hangover symptoms. The trade-off is that they irritate the stomach, and alcohol already does too. Take them with food and water. Read our guide to [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) before you combine them.
- **Acetaminophen** (Tylenol, CVS Health acetaminophen). Gentler on the stomach, but processed by the liver, which is still busy with alcohol. A single standard dose after the alcohol has cleared is generally considered reasonable for healthy people who don't drink heavily every day. It's a bad choice for anyone who drinks three or more drinks most days. Our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains the liver chemistry.
- **Aspirin** (Bayer, Ecotrin, store brand). Works for headaches but carries the same stomach-bleeding warning as other NSAIDs when combined with alcohol. See [aspirin and alcohol](/never-hungover/aspirin-and-alcohol).

If you can't decide between the two big options, our [Advil or Tylenol for a hangover](/never-hungover/advil-or-tylenol-for-hangover) comparison walks through it.

### Combination products (also in pain relief)

You'll see several products that combine a pain reliever with caffeine, an antacid, or both:

- **Alka-Seltzer Original** combines aspirin with sodium bicarbonate (baking soda) and citric acid in a fizzy tablet. The baking soda settles your stomach a little, and the aspirin handles the headache. It's a reasonable old-school choice, but it's still aspirin, and it's high in sodium. More in our [Alka-Seltzer for a hangover](/never-hungover/alka-seltzer-for-hangover) guide.
- **Excedrin** contains acetaminophen, aspirin, and caffeine together. That means two pain relievers with two different alcohol warnings in one tablet. It's good for migraine-type headaches, but read [Excedrin and alcohol](/never-hungover/excedrin-and-alcohol) before you reach for it after drinking.
- **Blowfish for Hangovers** is aspirin plus caffeine in a fizzy tablet, marketed specifically for hangovers. It's one of the few products with "hangover" on the box that's actually an FDA-regulated drug, and many pharmacies carry it. Our [Blowfish review](/never-hungover/blowfish-hangover-review) covers whether it's worth the premium over plain aspirin and a cup of coffee.

### Stomach products (the digestive health aisle)

- **Pepto-Bismol** and store-brand bismuth subsalicylate help with nausea, indigestion, and diarrhea. One catch: bismuth subsalicylate is chemically related to aspirin, so don't stack it with aspirin, Alka-Seltzer, Blowfish, or Excedrin. See [Pepto-Bismol and alcohol](/never-hungover/pepto-bismol-and-alcohol).
- **Tums** and other calcium carbonate antacids neutralize stomach acid quickly and are a simple fix for hangover heartburn. Details in [Tums and alcohol](/never-hungover/tums-and-alcohol).
- **Famotidine** (Pepcid AC and store brand) reduces acid production over several hours rather than neutralizing what's already there. It's useful if heartburn keeps coming back through the day.
- **Motion-sickness tablets** such as Dramamine can calm nausea, but most versions cause drowsiness and carry an alcohol warning. Wait until the alcohol is out of your system, and read [Dramamine and alcohol](/never-hungover/dramamine-and-alcohol) first.

### Supplements (the vitamin aisle)

CVS's vitamin aisle usually has B-complex vitamins, vitamin C, milk thistle, electrolyte tablets, and sometimes NAC or a branded "liver" or "recovery" blend. Some branches also carry a hangover-branded supplement or two. Most have little evidence behind them, and none is a cure.

## The Best Hangover Pills at Walgreens

The layout differs from CVS, but the categories and the advice are the same. A few things are specific to Walgreens.

Walgreens sells its own version of nearly every product above, and its ibuprofen, acetaminophen, naproxen, bismuth subsalicylate, antacid tablets, famotidine and oral electrolyte solution contain the same active ingredients at the same strengths as the name brands. The FDA holds over-the-counter drugs to the same active-ingredient standards whatever the label, so for the drugs in this guide the extra money for a name brand buys the logo.

Pedialyte, the Walgreens oral electrolyte solution, Liquid I.V. and sports drinks are usually all in stock. The store-brand solution is the cheapest per bottle.

Hangover-branded products come and go. Walgreens has carried various recovery drinks, shots and hangover supplements over the years, in stores and online. Whatever you find, read the ingredients before paying extra. Most are some mix of electrolytes, B vitamins, vitamin C, a pain reliever, or a botanical like milk thistle, prickly pear or ginger.

At either chain, the pharmacist can tell you in a minute, for free, whether a product clashes with your prescriptions. Ask if you take an antidepressant, a blood thinner, blood pressure or diabetes medicine, or anything for sleep or anxiety.

## Do CVS or Walgreens Sell DHM?

Rarely on the shelf. DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound, mostly extracted from vine tea and also found in the Japanese raisin tree (*Hovenia dulcis*), and it's sold as a dietary supplement rather than a drug. It isn't a standard item at most CVS or Walgreens branches. You may find a hangover formula that includes it, and both chains' websites sometimes list DHM from third-party sellers, but the choice is thin and changes often.

Most people who use DHM buy it online, where a 1,000 mg serving runs from $0.48 (NusaPure) to $2.92 (Cheers) depending on the brand. Our [DHM supplement reviews](/reviews) rank the brands we track, and you can [compare any two](/compare) on dose and price per serving.

Before you order, know what the research shows. A 2012 study by Shen and colleagues at UCLA, published in the *Journal of Neuroscience*, found DHM reduced signs of intoxication and withdrawal in rats, and later lab and animal work suggests it may help alcohol metabolism and the liver. Human evidence is much thinner, and there is no good evidence that DHM reliably prevents hangovers. It does nothing for judgment, driving or the risk of alcohol poisoning. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how people take it, and our [best hangover pills roundup](/never-hungover/best-hangover-pills) compares it with the other options.

## Products at CVS and Walgreens That Are Usually Not Worth It

Some things on the shelf are either overpriced versions of something cheaper or a poor fit for a hangover.

### "PM" and nighttime products

Tylenol PM, Advil PM, ZzzQuil, and store-brand sleep aids contain diphenhydramine or doxylamine, sedating antihistamines. Alcohol plus a sedating antihistamine adds up to more drowsiness, more confusion, and slower reactions, and the labels warn against combining them. If you've been drinking, skip these. It's tempting when you can't sleep after a night out, but our guide on [Benadryl for a hangover](/never-hungover/benadryl-for-hangover) explains why it backfires.

### Multi-symptom cold and flu products

DayQuil, NyQuil, and many cold and flu powders contain acetaminophen. If you've already taken Tylenol or Excedrin, a cold medicine can push you over the daily acetaminophen limit without you realizing. Some also contain alcohol-interacting ingredients like antihistamines or dextromethorphan. They're designed for colds, not hangovers.

### Expensive vitamin "hangover kits"

A blister pack of B vitamins and vitamin C with a hangover label usually costs more than a whole bottle of a store-brand B-complex. Alcohol can lower some B vitamins, and topping up is unlikely to hurt, but there's no good evidence that a vitamin pack prevents or treats a hangover on its own.

### Energy shots

Caffeine can take the edge off hangover fatigue, and a small amount may help a headache. But high-dose energy shots can make a racing heart, anxiety, or jitteriness worse, and those are already common the morning after. A cup of coffee or tea is cheaper and easier to dose.

## How to Avoid Doubling Up: The Ingredient Overlaps That Catch People Out

The most common mistake in the pharmacy the morning after is taking two products that share an active ingredient under different brand names. Check the "Active ingredients" box on the Drug Facts label of everything you buy.

| Ingredient | Where it turns up | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Acetaminophen | Tylenol (all versions), Excedrin, DayQuil, NyQuil, Theraflu and their store brands, many "PM" products, some prescription pain relievers | Two acetaminophen products at once can take you past the daily limit, and alcohol adds to the strain on the liver |
| Aspirin and other salicylates | Bayer, Ecotrin, Alka-Seltzer Original, Excedrin, Blowfish, BC and Goody's powders, Pepto-Bismol (as bismuth subsalicylate) | Each one adds to the risk of stomach bleeding |
| NSAIDs | Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), naproxen (Aleve), aspirin | Same drug family; don't combine them with each other |
| Sedating antihistamines | Anything labeled "PM," "night" or "sleep," plus Benadryl, Unisom and many motion-sickness and cold products | They add to alcohol's drowsiness |
| Caffeine | Excedrin, Blowfish, energy drinks, some "recovery" shots | It adds up with your morning coffee |

Pick one pain reliever, one stomach product if you need it, and an electrolyte drink. That covers most hangovers with no overlap.

## A Pharmacy Shopping List for the Morning After

For a healthy adult who drinks socially, this basket covers the common symptoms at low risk.

| What you're dealing with | What to buy | Cheaper option | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Thirst, dry mouth, dizziness when standing | Oral electrolyte solution or powder | CVS Health or Walgreens electrolyte solution | Very sugary drinks if your stomach is upset |
| Headache, body aches | Ibuprofen or naproxen with food, or a single dose of acetaminophen once alcohol has cleared | Store-brand ibuprofen or acetaminophen | Doubling up, empty stomach, heavy regular drinking |
| Heartburn, sour stomach | Calcium carbonate antacid or famotidine | Store-brand antacid tablets or famotidine | Taking antacids within a couple of hours of other medicines |
| Nausea, loose stool | Bismuth subsalicylate | Store-brand pink bismuth | Combining with aspirin products |
| Fatigue | Coffee or tea, food, rest | Coffee at home | High-dose energy shots, racing heart |

Add something to eat. Toast, crackers, bananas, eggs, or soup will often do more for how you feel than another product. A gentle meal raises low blood sugar, helps your stomach, and makes pain relievers easier to tolerate.

## Store Brand vs Name Brand: Is It Worth Paying More?

For the over-the-counter drugs in this guide, almost never. Store-brand ibuprofen, acetaminophen, naproxen, antacids, famotidine, and bismuth subsalicylate have to contain the same active ingredient at the stated strength as the name brand. Differences are usually in coatings, colors, flavors, and inactive ingredients. A few people prefer a specific brand's coating or taste, and that's a fine reason to pay more, but there's no medical reason to.

For electrolyte drinks, the store-brand oral rehydration solutions at both chains are typically formulated to closely match Pedialyte, at a lower price. Electrolyte powders like Liquid I.V. are more convenient to carry and taste better to many people, but compare the sodium content per serving if hydration is your main goal.

For supplements, "store brand vs name brand" matters more, because supplements are not tested by the FDA before sale. Look for a third-party quality seal, such as USP Verified or NSF, on whatever you buy, whether it's a store brand or not.

## Why No Pill Fully Fixes a Hangover

A hangover is several problems at once:

- dehydration and lost electrolytes, from alcohol's effect on your kidneys
- inflammation, as the immune system responds to alcohol and its by-products
- acetaldehyde, a toxic by-product your liver makes as it breaks down alcohol
- poor sleep, because alcohol disrupts the deeper stages of sleep later in the night
- an irritated stomach, from extra acid and direct irritation of the lining
- low blood sugar in some people, especially if they didn't eat
- congeners, compounds found in larger amounts in darker drinks like bourbon and red wine, which may make hangovers worse

Each pharmacy product targets one or two of these, which is why a few well-chosen basics plus food, water and sleep work better than any single "hangover pill." It's also why the only reliable way to avoid a bad hangover is to drink less, drink more slowly, eat before and during drinking, and alternate alcoholic drinks with water. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits that make the biggest difference.

## When to Skip the Pharmacy and See a Doctor

Most hangovers are miserable but harmless and fade within a day. But some symptoms after drinking aren't a hangover at all. Get medical care instead of buying another product if:

- **Someone can't be woken, is confused, or is breathing slowly or irregularly.** That's possible alcohol poisoning. Call 911 in the US.
- **You're vomiting repeatedly and can't keep fluids down for several hours**, or you see blood or material that looks like coffee grounds in your vomit. Persistent vomiting can cause serious dehydration, and blood can mean bleeding in the stomach.
- **You have black, tarry stools** after taking aspirin or NSAIDs with alcohol. (Bismuth subsalicylate can also turn stool black harmlessly, so mention it, but don't assume that's the reason.)
- **You have severe pain in your upper belly**, especially pain that spreads to your back, or pain under your right ribs, yellow skin or eyes, or dark urine.
- **You have chest pain, a very fast or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle, or fainting.**
- **Symptoms are getting worse after 24 hours** instead of better.
- **You notice shaking, sweating, anxiety, or a racing heart that shows up when you stop drinking after several days of heavy drinking.** Those can be alcohol withdrawal signs rather than a hangover, and withdrawal can become dangerous. Talk to a doctor plainly about how much you've been drinking. They can help you stop safely.
- **You think you took too much of a medicine**, or combined products with overlapping ingredients. Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 (US), even if you feel fine.

If you're not sure, the pharmacist at CVS or Walgreens can help you decide whether to see a doctor.

## Where DHM Fits If You Want to Try It

Since most pharmacies don't stock it, people who want to try DHM order it online. Its research is early and mostly in animals, there's no good evidence that it reliably prevents hangovers, and it's no reason to drink more.

For plain DHM, [Double Wood Supplements DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) has 1,000 mg per serving at $0.80, 30 servings to the bottle. If you'd rather have DHM blended with L-cysteine, milk thistle and electrolytes, [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) costs $1.93 a serving. If you take prescription medicine, ask your doctor or pharmacist first, and read every label before you combine a supplement with the pharmacy basics.

## The Bottom Line

CVS and Walgreens have everything you need to feel better after a night out, but almost none of it is labeled "hangover." Buy an electrolyte drink, one pain reliever matched to your stomach and your drinking habits, an antacid or bismuth product if your stomach is upset, and something to eat. Choose store brands to save money, read every Drug Facts label so you don't double up on acetaminophen or aspirin, and skip PM products, cold medicines, and pricey vitamin kits. If your symptoms look like alcohol poisoning, withdrawal, or bleeding, skip the pharmacy and get medical care. For a harder look at whether any of these products work at all, see [do hangover pills actually work?](/never-hungover/do-hangover-pills-actually-work)

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the best hangover pill at CVS?**

There isn't one product that treats a whole hangover. For most healthy adults, the most useful CVS purchase is an oral electrolyte solution (Pedialyte or the CVS Health version) plus a single pain reliever such as ibuprofen taken with food. Add an antacid or bismuth subsalicylate if your stomach is upset. Store brands contain the same active ingredients as name brands for less money.

**What hangover medicine does Walgreens sell?**

Walgreens sells the same categories as CVS: pain relievers (acetaminophen, ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin, Alka-Seltzer, Excedrin, and often Blowfish), stomach products (Pepto-Bismol, antacids, famotidine), electrolyte drinks and powders (Pedialyte, Walgreens oral electrolyte solution, Liquid I.V.), and vitamin and supplement products. Hangover-branded supplements vary by store, so check the Walgreens app for local stock.

**Does CVS or Walgreens sell DHM?**

DHM is not a standard shelf item at most CVS or Walgreens stores. You may find an occasional hangover formula that includes it, and the chains' websites sometimes list DHM products, but selection is limited and changes often. Most people buy DHM online. There is no good evidence that DHM reliably prevents hangovers, though early research is promising.

**Is Advil or Tylenol better for a hangover?**

Ibuprofen (Advil) is often more helpful for a hangover headache because inflammation plays a part in hangover symptoms, but it can irritate a stomach already upset by alcohol, so take it with food. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is easier on the stomach but adds work for the liver, so it's a poor choice for anyone who drinks heavily on a regular basis. Don't take either before or during drinking, and talk to a pharmacist if you're unsure.

**Are store-brand hangover medicines as good as name brands?**

For over-the-counter drugs, yes. Store-brand ibuprofen, acetaminophen, antacids, famotidine, and bismuth subsalicylate must contain the same active ingredient at the stated strength as the name brand. The store-brand electrolyte solutions at CVS and Walgreens are also formulated to closely match Pedialyte. Differences are mostly in inactive ingredients, coatings, and flavor.

**Can I take Pepto-Bismol and Alka-Seltzer together for a hangover?**

It's best not to. Pepto-Bismol contains bismuth subsalicylate, which is related to aspirin, and Alka-Seltzer Original contains aspirin. Taking both stacks salicylates, which adds to stomach-bleeding risk, especially after drinking. Pick one, or use a calcium carbonate antacid like Tums for heartburn instead, and ask the pharmacist if you're unsure.

**Do hangover pills from the pharmacy actually work?**

The over-the-counter drugs work for the specific symptom they treat: pain relievers ease headaches and aches, antacids ease heartburn, and electrolyte drinks help with dehydration. Hangover-branded supplements are a different story, and most have little good evidence behind them. No pharmacy product cures a hangover, and none makes drinking safer.

**When should I see a doctor instead of buying hangover medicine?**

Get care right away if someone can't stay awake, is confused, or is breathing slowly, which can mean alcohol poisoning. Also see a doctor for repeated vomiting that won't stop, blood in vomit or black stools, severe belly pain, yellow skin or eyes, chest pain, a racing heart that won't settle, or symptoms that get worse after a day. Shaking and sweating after stopping several days of heavy drinking can be withdrawal, which needs medical advice.
